newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Ex-Fed official sees intermeeting hike.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ex-Fed official sees intermeeting hike.

text.p: Former Federal Reserve Board Staff Director Stephen Axilrod on Thursday said the U.S. central bank likely maintained a bias to tighten credit and may raise interest rates at the first signs of inflationary pressure.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), of which Axilrod had been the Secretary, met Tuesday and Wednesday and decided to leave the federal funds rate unchanged at 5.25 percent.
"Sure, I think there is an asymmetric directive with the possibility of a move before the next FOMC meeting if the economy shows some steam," Axilrod told Reuters.

In July, the policy-setting commmittee adopted a directive toward tightening credit that was reinstated at each meeting through December, the last meeting for which minutes were made available on Thursday.

The minutes of this week's meeting will be released in late March. The FOMC, which last lowered the federal funds rate by 25 basis points on January 31, 1996, will next meet on March 27. The Fed's tightening bias has been in place for at least seven straight months and has not prompted a Fed action -- by far the longest stretch under Chairman Alan Greenspan.
The bias coincided with a Fed forecast for a slowdown that did not materialize in the second half of 1996. The Gross Domestic Product rose by 4.7 percent in October-December.

"It's a given there is going to be some slowdown from the fourth quarter," said Axilrod, who is now an adviser to consulting firm MFR Inc. "But even with a slowdown, if there are signs of cost pressure, the Fed will not wait to move."

Axilrod said that he expected January data to be released over the next 10 days will provide some sense of where inflation is headed, thereby setting the stage for Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before Congress later this month.

Among the key reports the Fed looks at, Axilrod singled out the employment report, due out on Friday -- and mainly its average hourly earnings component -- as well as next week's retail sales and industrial production.
The former Fed official, however, did not expect the Fed to move following the employment report alone -- but rather on the broader picture of the economy.

"Growth in December was high, so that if you just extrapolate the levels, you probably have a fairly strong first quarter," he said. "The employment can give a hint of what happens in the first quarter."
Axilrod also believed the Fed was close to a tightening five months ago, "but not quite there."

"They backed away from (a tightening), and now, it is sort of obvious they are talking about it a little more," Axilrod said. Policymakers "surely" must have come closer to raising rates this week compared to their position over the last five months, he added.

The former Fed official said the current economic picture shows some reason to hike short-term rates, but noted "a compelling scenario" does not yet exist. The presence of a tightening bias, he added, offers "a reasonable compromise."
Axilrod, who took part in the 1985 Plaza Accord to lower the dollar, described the U.S. currency's strength as "a very, very marginal factor in (formulating monetary) policy."
